commentary.text:
Red claims a central square immediately, establishing a safe foothold that cannot be captured in one move and supporting our center-occupation route.
```memo
### Position read
Opening position. Red has advanced from (0,3) to (3,3), taking the upper-left center. It is not immediately sandwichable because neither opponent color has a matching far flank.

### Our plan
Use Yellow to reinforce or claim another center square, while developing same-color pairs that can punish opposing center entries. Prioritize immediate center threats, but verify every exposed line against both opposing turns.

### Opponent tendencies
No moves observed yet. Watch whether the opponent races into the center or builds same-color flanks along rows 3–4.

### Lessons
Captures require same-color flanks and trigger only from the landing square. A piece may safely move into an existing sandwich.
```

I’m occupying (3,4) beside the opponent’s advanced center piece. This immediately blocks a center victory and gives us a durable foothold while Green prepares to contest the lower central squares.
```memo
### Position read
The opponent opened by advancing an edge piece to (3,3). We answered with our right-edge piece to (3,4), splitting the upper center. No losses or eliminations have occurred.

### Our plan
Keep at least one center square secured while bringing our left-edge color toward (4,3) or (4,4). Look for same-color sandwich setups; never assume our two colors can flank together. Avoid friendly-fire lines through our own teammate.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent immediately prioritized direct center occupation, suggesting a fast center race.

### Lessons
A center foothold prevents an instant four-square occupation and forces the opponent to dislodge us. Recalculate captures only from each landing square.
```

Yellow takes the lower-left center, denying Green access while preserving Red’s forced sandwich: next turn, Red can land at (3,5) and capture the Blue piece between two Reds.
```memo
### Position read
We hold center squares (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; Blue occupies (3,4). Yellow at (4,3) cannot be immediately sandwiched because the opponent lacks a same-color far flank. Green cannot prevent Red’s available sandwich from (0,5) to (3,5): Blue (3,4) lies between Red pieces at (3,3) and the landing square.

### Our plan
Unless Green creates a higher-priority threat, play Red (0,5)→(3,5), capturing Blue at (3,4). Then contest the remaining center squares while supporting occupants with same-color flank geometry. Recheck for any immediate opponent center win or multi-capture first.

### Opponent tendencies
Blue raced directly into the center at (3,4), adjacent to our Red without same-color support, allowing a prepared sandwich. Watch for Green entering (4,4) or staging lines against our Yellow.

### Lessons
A center race should be paired with tactical flank scans. Teammate center pieces coordinate occupation but cannot serve as same-color sandwich endpoints.
```

We block the opponent’s immediate move from (0,5) to (3,5), which would sandwich and capture our center piece at (3,4). The piece on (2,5) also develops toward the center while preserving our tactical lanes.
```memo
### Position read
We hold (3,4); the opponent holds (3,3) and (4,3). Our new piece at (2,5) blocks the direct descent from (0,5) to (3,5), preventing an immediate same-color sandwich of our center piece. No losses or eliminations yet.

### Our plan
Preserve (3,4) and contest the last center square. Consider placing one of our center-holder color at (5,3), then later moving another to (2,3): if the opponent leaves pieces at (3,3) and (4,3), that same-color sandwich captures both. Keep (5,3) and its approach lane clear.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is racing both colors directly into adjacent central squares and may seek a same-color flank around our blocker.

### Lessons
Before every move, scan for one-move sandwiches against occupied center squares. A blocker anywhere on a rook path can prevent the capturing landing square from being reached.
```

I’m placing Red on the center’s right flank. This threatens to sandwich the unsupported Blue center piece between our Reds at (3,3) and (3,6), forcing the opponent either to vacate the center or spend Green’s move blocking the capture lane.
```memo
### Position read
We hold (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; Blue holds (3,4). Green’s move to (2,5) blocked the direct Red descent to (3,5). Red now occupies (3,6), creating a threatened landing at (3,5) that would sandwich Blue (3,4) against Red (3,3). No current losses.

### Our plan
If Blue remains at (3,4) and (3,5) is empty on Red’s next turn, play Red (3,6)→(3,5) to capture it. Expect Green (2,5)→(3,5) as a possible block; use Yellow’s intervening move to improve center control or constrain that blocker. If Blue vacates, aim to occupy (3,4) and (4,4) while preserving both existing center pieces.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent uses Green to obstruct prepared Red capture lanes and Blue to race into center. Recheck Green’s mobility around columns 4-6 before assuming a sandwich remains available.

### Lessons
A threatened sandwich can force a center evacuation even when an immediate capture is blocked. Account for the opponent’s second color inserting a piece on the intended landing square.
```

I’m securing the critical fifth file so Yellow cannot occupy (3,5) from below. This preserves Green’s next move from (2,5) to (3,5), which will block Red’s immediate sandwich threat against our center piece.
```memo
### Position read
We hold (3,4); the opponent holds (3,3) and (4,3). Red at (3,6) threatens to move to (3,5), sandwiching our center piece against Red at (3,3). Our Blue move to (4,5) blocks Yellow's direct route from (7,5) toward (3,5). No losses or eliminations yet.

### Our plan
On Green's turn, if legal, move Green (2,5) to (3,5), physically blocking Red's capturing landing square. Then preserve the Blue center holder and seek a same-color flank against Red at (3,6). Blue can later establish at (3,7), and after Green vacates (3,5), a Blue move from (3,4) to (3,5) would capture Red at (3,6).

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is concentrating both colors in and around the center and has begun creating same-color sandwich geometry rather than merely occupying squares.

### Lessons
Defend threatened pieces by controlling the attacker's landing square. Account for intervening opponent turns: blocking Yellow's access to (3,5) makes the intended Green defense more reliable.
```

Yellow reinforces our center majority, occupying (4,4) while preserving both existing central pieces. This creates three-square control and keeps pressure on Blue at (3,4), which Red may still sandwich unless Green blocks (3,5).
```memo
### Position read
We occupy three center squares: Red (3,3), Yellow (4,3) and Yellow (4,4); Blue occupies the fourth at (3,4). Red at (3,6) threatens to land (3,5) and sandwich Blue against Red (3,3), but Green at (2,5) can occupy (3,5) first. Blue also sits at (4,5). No losses.

### Our plan
Center victory is one Blue removal away. If Green does not block (3,5), play Red (3,6)→(3,5) to capture Blue (3,4) and win immediately. If Green blocks there, preserve the three center occupants and look for a Red maneuver that clears or bypasses the blocker. Avoid moving any center piece unless required to prevent a capture or immediate loss.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent uses Green to obstruct prepared Red sandwich landings and Blue to contest the center. Expect Green (2,5)→(3,5), then watch for Blue attempts to attack the Yellow center pair.

### Lessons
Three stable center occupants create a forcing threat, but the empty capture landing must be defended against obstruction. Recheck every opponent rook lane into (3,5) and the center before committing.
```

I occupy (3,5) with Green, denying Red the landing square needed to sandwich our Blue center piece. This also reinforces our center presence while keeping the planned Blue counter-capture geometry available.
```memo
### Position read
We hold (3,4) with Blue and now (3,5) with Green. The opponent holds (3,3), (4,3), and (4,4), so the center remains contested. Green at (3,5) blocks Red at (3,6) from landing there and sandwiching our Blue piece against Red at (3,3). No losses or eliminations yet.

### Our plan
Preserve our two adjacent pieces on row 3 and prevent the opponent from completing the center. Seek Blue same-color flanking geometry against Red at (3,6), potentially by establishing Blue at (3,7). If Green later vacates (3,5), Blue may move from (3,4) to (3,5) to capture Red at (3,6), provided a Blue far flank exists.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is concentrating both colors in the center and using Red pieces on row 3 to threaten sandwiches. Yellow has advanced directly into (4,4), increasing the urgency of center denial.

### Lessons
An occupied attack square can stop an otherwise immediate sandwich. Always check whether moving that blocker later exposes the protected piece, and watch for instant center victory after every move.
```

I preserve our three center occupants while lifting the Red flank to safety. This keeps pressure on the contested center line and leaves Yellow’s immediate threat of (7,6)→(4,6), which would sandwich Blue at (4,5) against Yellow (4,4).
```memo
### Position read
We hold Red (3,3) and Yellow (4,3),(4,4); Blue holds (3,4), Green blocks at (3,5), and Blue at (4,5) is exposed to Yellow (7,6)→(4,6). Red moved from (3,6) to (2,6), preserving all center occupants while retaining the option to return to (3,6).

### Our plan
On Yellow’s turn, capture Blue (4,5) with (7,6)→(4,6) if it remains. If Blue escapes, develop a spare Yellow without moving the three center holders. A later Red return to (3,6) captures the contiguous Green/Blue center line only if Green has not opened a gap. After clearing (3,4), we must still occupy it to win.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent uses Green (3,5) as a movable shield for Blue (3,4). Expect Blue to evacuate (4,5), then Green either to retain the blockade or move to break Red’s sandwich geometry.

### Lessons
Removing the opponent from a center square does not itself complete center occupation; the vacated square must be filled. Preserve the three established center pieces while creating a safe route for a spare piece into (3,4).
```

Blue converts the central alignment into an immediate sandwich: landing at (5,4) traps Yellow on (4,4) against our Blue piece at (3,4). This breaks the opponent’s three-square center formation and inflicts the first loss.
```memo
### Position read
Blue moved (5,7) to (5,4), sandwiching and capturing Yellow at (4,4) against Blue at (3,4). Yellow now has 1 loss; all other loss counts are 0. After the capture, the center has opponent pieces at (3,3) and (4,3), our Blue at (3,4), and (4,4) empty. Green remains at (3,5), protecting the row-3 structure.

### Our plan
Keep denying center occupation while exploiting same-color flanks. Blue at (3,4) and (5,4) create vertical capture potential if an opponent enters (4,4): a future Blue move cannot capture merely because the sandwich exists, so we must trigger it by landing elsewhere appropriately or re-forming the line. Green should maintain pressure beside the center and avoid exposing Blue at (3,4).

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent has concentrated both colors around the four central squares. Expect Yellow to refill (4,4) or reposition from (4,3), and Red to seek a way around Green’s blocker at (3,5).

### Lessons
Look for captures formed by an existing friendly far flank: landing at (5,4) used Blue at (3,4) to remove the intervening center piece. Captures require our triggering move; static sandwiches do nothing.
```

I’m blocking Green’s immediate entry along row 3. Without this move, Green could land beside our Red center piece and sandwich the entire Red–Blue line against Green’s piece on (3,5); Yellow on (3,1) closes that route while preserving our two current center occupants.
```memo
### Position read
We hold Red (3,3) and Yellow (4,3); Blue holds center (3,4). Blue captured our Yellow at (4,4), raising Yellow to 1 loss. Green at (3,0) threatened to land on (3,2) and capture Red (3,3) plus Blue (3,4) against Green (3,5). Yellow moved (7,1)→(3,1), blocking Green’s row-3 approach.

### Our plan
Preserve the center holders and rebuild occupation of (4,4). On Red’s next turn, if Green remains at (3,5), consider (2,6)→(3,6), which sandwiches Green (3,5) and Blue (3,4) against Red (3,3). After (3,4) is cleared, route a spare piece there while maintaining (3,3),(4,3),(4,4). Watch Blue’s vertical pair at (3,4)/(5,4), which can capture anything between them when one flank moves into place.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent uses mixed-color center lines tactically and exploited Blue’s same-color vertical flanks to capture Yellow (4,4). Green is likely to move (3,5) now to avoid Red’s return capture.

### Lessons
Before contesting center occupation, scan mixed lines for a same-color far flank. Blocking the mover’s landing corridor can neutralize a multi-capture without disturbing established center pieces.
```

Green steps to (2,5) to break Red’s dangerous row-3 sandwich threat against both central defenders. If Red captures this Green against its piece at (2,6), Blue can answer by sandwiching that Red piece vertically.
```memo
### Position read
Our Green moved (3,5) to (2,5), defusing the immediate opponent move (2,6)→(3,6), which would have sandwiched and captured our pieces at (3,5) and (3,4) against the opponent at (3,3). Center remains: opponent at (3,3),(4,3), ours at (3,4), and (4,4) empty. Losses: opponent Yellow 1, all others 0.

### Our plan
If the opponent plays (0,4)→(2,4), capturing our Green at (2,5) against its (2,6), answer on Blue’s turn with (1,7)→(1,4): the landing sandwiches the new opponent piece at (2,4) against our Blue at (3,4). Continue denying all-opponent center occupation while building same-color flanks.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is concentrating around the center and may prioritize tactical sandwiches involving the piece at (3,3). Watch moves landing on row 3 to exploit that far flank.

### Lessons
Mixed-color lines are capturable when bounded by one moving color. Evacuating the adjacent piece can break a dangerous line; choose the evacuation square to create a recapture if pursued.
```

I’m shifting the advanced Red to (3,6), creating a same-color flank with Red at (3,3). If Blue remains at (3,4), Red can land on (3,5) next turn and capture it; moving Blue to (4,4) would allow Yellow (7,6)→(4,6) to capture both Blue center-row pieces.
```memo
### Position read
We hold Red (3,3), Yellow (3,1)/(4,3); Blue holds (3,4). Red moved (2,6)→(3,6), so (3,6)→(3,5) captures Blue (3,4) against Red (3,3) if Blue stays. Yellow has 1 loss; all others have 0.

### Our plan
Exploit the forced Blue retreat from (3,4). If Blue moves to (4,4), Yellow (7,6)→(4,6) sandwiches Blue at (4,5) and (4,4) against Yellow (4,3), a double capture. If Blue retreats vertically upward, use the freed (3,4) while preserving Red (3,3), then rebuild toward all four centers. Watch Green (2,5) potentially moving to (3,5) as a blocker.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent has defended center tactically and moved Green away from the threatened row-3 sandwich. Expect Blue to retreat to (2,4) or (1,4), avoiding both Red’s capture and Yellow’s double-capture geometry.

### Lessons
Same-color flanks can force a center holder away even without an immediate capture. Always scan the teammate’s next move: Yellow’s (4,3)/(7,6) alignment makes Blue’s apparent refuge at (4,4) dangerous.
```

I slide the Blue piece from (4,5) into the last empty center square. This secures both right-hand center squares while vacating (4,5), so Yellow cannot use (7,6)→(4,6) to sandwich two Blue pieces against Yellow at (4,3).
```memo
### Position read
We moved Blue (4,5)→(4,4). The center is fully occupied but split: opponent at (3,3),(4,3), ours at (3,4),(4,4), so neither team wins. Vacating (4,5) prevents the opponent’s Yellow (7,6)→(4,6) from sandwiching our center pair. Losses: opponent Yellow 1; all others 0.

### Our plan
Protect our Blue at (3,4) from opponent Red (3,6)→(3,5), which would capture it against Red (3,3). On Green’s turn, if (3,5) is empty, strongly consider Green (2,5)→(3,5) to block that landing; moving into the bracket is safe. If the opponent occupies (3,5), it already blocks the Red capture. Hold both right center squares and seek same-color flanks against the opponent’s two left-center pieces.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent concentrates pieces around the center and builds same-color sandwich endpoints. Check every accessible landing beside our central pieces, especially rows 3 and 4.

### Lessons
Before filling a gap between pieces, inspect whether it completes an opponent sandwich line. Moving the former endpoint into the gap can gain occupation while breaking the dangerous line.
```

Blue’s shift to (4,4) leaves it exposed against Yellow’s central anchor. Yellow lands on (4,5), capturing that Blue piece and clearing a center square while retaining pressure on Blue at (3,4).
```memo
### Position read
Yellow moved (7,5)→(4,5), sandwiching Blue (4,4) against Yellow (4,3). Blue now has 1 loss; Yellow has 1. We hold centers (3,3) Red and (4,3) Yellow; Blue still holds (3,4), while (4,4) is empty. Red (3,6) threatens to land (3,5) and capture Blue (3,4) against Red (3,3).

### Our plan
Preserve the row-3 Red flank and clear Blue from (3,4). If Green does not occupy (3,5), execute Red (3,6)→(3,5). Yellow at (4,5) is positioned to enter (4,4) later; after clearing and occupying (3,4), this creates a direct center-win route. If Green blocks (3,5), seek another Red landing that restores the sandwich rather than sacrificing central anchors.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent chose Blue (4,5)→(4,4), avoiding the predicted double capture but allowing an immediate single capture. Green (2,5)→(3,5) is the most natural defensive reply because it blocks Red’s landing square.

### Lessons
When a retreat vacates the intended landing square, check whether another same-color piece can land there immediately; Yellow (7,5) converted the altered geometry into a clean capture.
```

I’m blocking the immediate Red landing on (3,5), which would otherwise sandwich our remaining upper-center Blue against Red at (3,3). This also preserves our split control of the center and establishes a Green endpoint on row 3 for future sandwich tactics.
```memo
### Position read
We moved Green (2,5)→(3,5), blocking Red (3,6)→(3,5), which would have captured our Blue at (3,4) against Red (3,3). Center: opponent holds (3,3),(4,3); we hold (3,4); (4,4) is empty. Losses: our Blue 1, opponent Yellow 1, others 0.

### Our plan
If still safe on Blue’s turn, consider Blue (5,4)→(4,4) to restore both right-center squares. Green endpoints now sit at (3,0) and (3,5); landing a Green at (3,2) would sandwich Yellow (3,1) leftward and the mixed Red (3,3)+Blue (3,4) rightward, trading one Blue loss for losses to both opponent colors. First determine whether that friendly-fire trade is worthwhile and whether the opponent disrupts the row.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is actively using same-color endpoints near the center; Yellow used (4,3) to capture our Blue at (4,4). Expect attempts to reopen (3,5) or build another bracket around our center pieces.

### Lessons
A blocking piece may both prevent an immediate sandwich and become a far endpoint for a later multi-direction capture. Recheck all four rays after every central move, including friendly-fire costs.
```

Blue can otherwise play (2,7)→(3,7), sandwiching our Red at (3,6) and Green at (3,5) against Blue (3,4). I’m withdrawing the exposed Red upward while keeping it near the center for redeployment.
```memo
### Position read
We hold centers (3,3) Red and (4,3) Yellow; the opponent holds (3,4), and (4,4) is empty. Green blocked our planned Red landing at (3,5). Our Red at (3,6) was exposed to Blue (2,7)→(3,7), which would sandwich it and Green (3,5) against Blue (3,4), so Red withdrew to (2,6). Losses: we have Red 0, Yellow 1; opponent Blue 1, Green 0.

### Our plan
Protect the two central anchors and look for a safe way to clear Blue (3,4). Red (2,6) remains mobile near the center. Yellow (4,5) can contest (4,4), but Blue entering (4,4) between our two Yellow pieces is safe until a Yellow flank can move away and return. Avoid leaving mixed lines that let one opponent color capture several pieces.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent used Green (2,5)→(3,5) to block the immediate sandwich of Blue (3,4). Expect Blue to reinforce or relocate its central piece, especially toward (4,4), and Green to keep obstructing Red’s row-3 geometry.

### Lessons
After a capture threat is blocked, scan beyond the blocker: Blue had a counter-sandwich landing at (3,7) that made the advanced Red flank unsafe.
```

I’m restoring our second central foothold. This blocks an easy center takeover while keeping both Blue center pieces mutually supported and uncaptured.
```memo
### Position read
We moved Blue (5,4)→(4,4). Center now has opponent pieces at (3,3),(4,3) and ours at (3,4),(4,4). Losses: our Blue 1; opponent Yellow 1; others 0. Red retreated from (3,6) to (2,6), leaving Green (3,5) in place.

### Our plan
Preserve the two right-center squares and watch for Yellow attempts to dislodge Blue (4,4). On Green’s turn, seek moves that constrain the opponent’s two left-center pieces without exposing our Blue pieces to same-color brackets. Build reachable Green endpoints before attempting a row-3 sandwich.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is actively contesting the center and previously used Yellow endpoints to capture Blue at (4,4). Red withdrew when its direct row-3 capture route was blocked.

### Lessons
The earlier proposed Green landing at (3,2) is currently impossible: pieces at (3,4) and (3,3) block Green from (3,5), while Yellow at (3,1) blocks Green from (3,0). Always verify the entire travel path before planning a sandwich.
```

Yellow steps back while keeping our center anchor intact. Returning to (4,5) will sandwich Blue on (4,4) against Yellow (4,3), forcing the opponent to block the landing or withdraw that central piece.
```memo
### Position read
We hold centers (3,3) Red and (4,3) Yellow; Blue holds (3,4) and (4,4). Losses: Red 0, Yellow 1; Blue 1, Green 0. Yellow moved (4,5)→(5,5), leaving the central anchor in place and creating a direct return-sandwich threat against Blue (4,4).

### Our plan
On the next Yellow turn, (5,5)→(4,5) captures Blue (4,4) against Yellow (4,3) if the lane remains open. Green can block (4,5) from (3,5), but then Yellow (7,6)→(4,6) threatens to capture the blocker and Blue together if Blue stays. Expect Blue to retreat from (4,4); then consolidate the vacated center and seek a safe attack on Blue (3,4). Protect Yellow, already at 1 loss.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent uses Green to obstruct same-color sandwich landings and Blue to reinforce the center. Expect Green (3,5)→(4,5) or another interference, followed by Blue evacuating (4,4).

### Lessons
A supported return-square threat can force a central retreat without vacating our own center anchor. Check whether a blocker creates an alternate multi-capture lane.
```

I pull the exposed Green piece to (1,5), where it blocks Red’s vertical route to (3,5). This preserves our upper-center Blue piece; the lower-center piece remains under pressure, but blocking that attack instead would permit a devastating coordinated capture of both center pieces.
```memo
### Position read
We moved (3,5)→(1,5). The center remains split: the opponent occupies (3,3),(4,3), while we occupy (3,4),(4,4). Our piece at (1,5) blocks the opponent’s top-edge piece from landing at (3,5), so the upper-center piece cannot be immediately sandwiched. Losses remain ours 1, opponent 1.

### Our plan
Expect the opponent to capture our piece at (4,4) by landing at (4,5); preserve the piece at (3,4) and then contest the vacated lower-center square. Use the advanced piece at (1,5) to constrain the top edge or descend again when the central file clears.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent coordinates same-color endpoints carefully and attacks occupied center squares immediately when a landing square opens. They withdrew a direct upper capture threat only to retain another route.

### Lessons
Moving to (4,5) would fail: the opponent could first capture (3,4), then land at (4,6) and sandwich both (4,5) and (4,4). When defending one center square, check whether the blocker completes a longer opposing sandwich.
```

I’m taking the exposed Green piece while creating a fork on Blue’s center: Red can next land at (3,5) to sandwich Blue at (3,4), while Yellow already threatens the same treatment at (4,4). Blue can move only one of those pieces before Yellow acts.
```memo
### Position read
Red (2,6)→(2,5) captures Green (1,5) against Red (0,5), making losses Red 0, Yellow 1, Blue 1, Green 1. We still hold centers (3,3) Red and (4,3) Yellow; Blue holds (3,4) and (4,4).

### Our plan
Blue's center is forked. Yellow (5,5)→(4,5) sandwiches Blue (4,4) against Yellow (4,3). If Blue saves that piece, Red (2,5)→(3,5) next turn sandwiches Blue (3,4) against Red (3,3). If Blue saves (3,4), execute the Yellow capture. Recheck Green's intervening move for any new blocker or counter-capture, but no current Green piece appears able to reach either landing square immediately.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent had used Green to obstruct center capture lanes, but moved the key blocker from (3,5) to (1,5), where it was capturable. Expect Blue to evacuate one center piece and Green to seek interference with the remaining threat.

### Lessons
Coordinate same-color flanks across both rows: simultaneous Red and Yellow sandwich threats can overload the opponent's single Blue turn.
```

Red’s capture reopened the attack on both Blue center pieces. I’m saving the lower one by stepping onto Yellow’s intended landing square; this also threatens to sandwich the Yellow piece at (5,5) with (6,7)→(6,5).
```memo
### Position read
We moved our lower-center piece from (4,4) to (4,5). Our piece at (3,4) remains exposed: the opponent can land at (3,5) from (2,5) and sandwich it against (3,3). Losses are currently ours 2 total across our colors and the opponent 1.

### Our plan
Our piece at (4,5) blocks the immediate lower sandwich and threatens the opponent piece at (5,5): moving our piece from (6,7) to (6,5) would capture it against (4,5). Use the next move of our other color to improve central access, though it cannot presently stop the upper-center capture. Preserve the surviving normal piece because one more loss would eliminate that color.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent rapidly removes blockers to reopen coordinated same-color sandwich routes. Expect them to move the threatened piece at (5,5), or accept its loss while preparing a counter-sandwich around (4,5).

### Lessons
When two center pieces are both under sequential capture, save the one whose escape square also creates tempo. A defensive landing can be stronger when it denies the attack square and establishes a sandwich threat.
```

I’m shielding the Yellow piece on (5,5) from Blue’s sandwich threat: placing Yellow on (6,6) blocks Blue’s route from (6,7) to (6,5). This preserves our tactical reply if the remaining central Blue shifts to (4,4), while Red remains poised to capture Blue on (3,4).
```memo
### Position read
Yellow (7,6)→(6,6) blocks Blue (6,7) from reaching (6,5), preventing a sandwich of Yellow (5,5) against Blue (4,5). Losses remain Red 0, Yellow 1, Blue 1, Green 1. Centers: Red (3,3), Blue (3,4), Yellow (4,3), with (4,4) empty.

### Our plan
After the opponent's Green turn, Red (2,5)→(3,5) should sandwich Blue (3,4) against Red (3,3), raising Blue to 2 losses. If Blue then moves (4,5)→(4,4), Yellow (5,5)→(4,5) captures it against Yellow (4,3), eliminating Blue. If Blue evacuates elsewhere, use the cleared center and keep Yellow (5,5) safe.

### Opponent tendencies
Blue retreats endangered center pieces and may use edge pieces for remote sandwich landings. Green may try to obstruct Red's landing square, though no current Green has a direct route to (3,5).

### Lessons
Check distant rook landings before preserving a tactical piece: blocking Blue's (6,7)→(6,5) route keeps the Yellow center-capture mechanism intact.
```

I’m developing Green onto column 4, preparing to enter (3,4) after Red’s likely sandwich removes the Blue piece there. This secures a route toward the upper center while avoiding the immediate Yellow sandwich traps around rows 4–5.
```memo
### Position read
We moved the acting piece from (1,0) to (1,4), opening a direct route down column 4. The opponent can now move (2,5) to (3,5), sandwiching our piece at (3,4) against (3,3); that would raise that color's losses to 2. The opponent's latest piece at (6,6) blocks our former capture route from (6,7) to (6,5).
```
